posts.caption:
Why is String immutable in Java? 🤔

Most developers answer "security" and stop there. That's only 1 of the 4 reasons interviewers expect:

✅ String Pool: literals are shared safely
✅ Security: paths, URLs and credentials can't be swapped
✅ Cached hashCode: the perfect HashMap key
✅ Thread safety: share across threads without locks

Bonus: because String is immutable, s += x inside a loop creates a new object every time. Use StringBuilder instead.

💬 Quick question: can you break String immutability using reflection? Should you?

== vs equals() in Java: the classic interview trap ⚠️

new String("CJD") == new String("CJD") → false
"CJD" == "CJD" → true

Same text, different answers. Why?

🔹 == compares references (same object?)
🔹 equals() compares content (same value?)
🔹 String literals come from the String Pool, so == "works" by accident

✅ Use equals() for objects
✅ Use Objects.equals() for null safety
✅ Override hashCode() whenever you override equals()

String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer: pick the wrong one and your loop gets slow 🐢

🔸 String: immutable, a new object on every change
🔸 StringBuilder: mutable, fastest, not thread-safe
🔸 StringBuffer: mutable, thread-safe (synchronized), slower

A 10,000-iteration loop with s += i creates 10,000 throwaway Strings. One StringBuilder does it with a single buffer.

➡️ Fixed text → String
➡️ Building text → StringBuilder
➡️ Shared across threads → StringBuffer

posts.caption:
String Pool & intern(): how Java saves memory 🧠

Write "CJD" 1,000 times in your code and Java stores it only once.

🔹 String literals go to the String Pool (in the heap since Java 7)
🔹 new String("CJD") always creates a separate object
🔹 intern() returns the pooled copy

✅ Use intern() for heavily repeated runtime values (city, status, country codes)
❌ Don't use it just to make == work. Use equals().

💬 Interview classic: how many objects does new String("CJD") create, 1 or 2?
